title: The Irreplaceable Interpreter
author: The Last Analogue
summary: The Last Analogue applies Charles Sanders Peirce's semiotic triad -- sign, object, interpretant -- to AI and education, arguing that the student's act of interpretation is not a step that AI can shortcut but the irreducible outcome that education exists to produce. Remove the student's interpretant and you do not have a more efficient system -- you have a different system entirely. The article's central claim is that AI tutoring systems fundamentally alter the semiotic situation in education. When AI interprets a text for a student, it does not assist interpretation -- it substitutes its own interpretant for the student's. The student receives the AI's meaning, not their own. On Peircean terms, this is a fundamental category error. The irreplaceability of the student-as-interpreter is not a sentimental claim about human specialness but a structural claim about what interpretation is. Interpretation is an act performed by a particular mind in a particular historical and relational situation. It cannot be outsourced without ceasing to be that student's interpretation. What is lost is the formation of the student as a meaning-making subject. The practical implication is not a rejection of AI in education but a clarification of what AI can legitimately do: expand available texts, provide scaffolding, and model interpretive moves -- but the interpretation itself must remain the student's act, or the educational purpose is defeated from within.
points: Peirce's semiotic triad reveals that interpretation is the constitutive act of understanding itself -- the interpretant cannot be pre-supplied without eliminating the educational transaction.

When an AI system interprets a text for a student, it performs a category substitution: replacing the student's interpretant with its own, producing a student who has received a meaning rather than made one -- the structural inverse of education's purpose.

The irreplaceability of the student-interpreter is a logical consequence of what interpretation is -- an act of a particular mind in a particular situation -- not merely a humanist sentiment about current AI limitations.
AI can legitimately serve as a sign-expander, scaffolding mechanism, or interpretive model, but not as a substitute interpretant without defeating the purpose it purports to serve.

The deepest risk of AI in education is not wrong answers but right answers: habituating students to received meaning atrophies the capacity for original interpretation that education exists to cultivate.
quotes: I came across Charles Sanders Peirce's theory of signs and found in it not a philosophical curiosity but a precise diagnosis of what is at stake when we ask an AI to help a student understand a text.

In Peirce's system, the interpretant is not the person doing the interpreting. It is the meaning-effect produced in that person by their encounter with the sign. It is irreducibly theirs. It cannot be pre-formed by another mind and delivered intact. The moment you deliver it, it becomes your interpretant, not theirs.

When a student asks an AI to explain what a poem means and the AI explains, the student does not receive an interpretation. They receive the AI's interpretant. They now possess a meaning they did not make. This is not learning. This is, in the most precise sense, the opposite of learning.

The question is not whether AI interpretations are accurate. They often are. The question is what kind of mind is formed by a childhood of receiving accurate interpretations rather than struggling toward imperfect ones.

Peirce saw that semiosis -- the process of meaning-making -- is never finished. Every interpretant becomes a new sign, which calls forth a new interpretant, in an infinite chain of meaning-making. Education is the deliberate cultivation of this capacity.

The teacher's irreplaceability is not sentimental. It is structural. The teacher is the third term in the semiotic relation -- the one whose presence transforms the sign-object encounter into an occasion for the student's interpretant to form.
